summary: Defines how an IS-IS router advertises supported Maximum SID Depths at node or link level, so controllers can tell whether a given SID stack can be supported in a segment routing network.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 8491 lets an IS-IS router say how many labels it can push onto a packet. A controller that builds paths needs that number, because a path asking for more labels than a router can carry will fail. The router publishes one number for the whole device and, if it differs, one number for each link. The document also creates the registry that defines what each kind of depth means.

questions: what is base mpls imposition msd
subtitle: How an IS-IS router tells controllers how deep a stack of segment identifiers it can push onto a packet.

tldr.problem: A controller that computes Segment Routing paths needs to know how many segment identifiers each node on the path can handle, or the path it computes may be impossible to carry.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds a Node MSD sub-TLV to the IS-IS Router CAPABILITY TLV and a Link MSD sub-TLV to the link advertisements, each holding one or more pairs of an MSD type and a value between 0 and 255. It also creates the IGP MSD-Types registry and defines the Base MPLS Imposition type.
tldr.outcome: Every IS-IS router in the network can publish its depth, and a controller can check a computed path against it before the path is installed. A wrong value causes either a path that cannot be computed or a path that cannot be carried.

facts.label: TLVs that may carry the Link MSD

today: RFC 8491 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. It allocates the Node MSD sub-TLV type 23 and the Link MSD sub-TLV type 15, and it creates the IGP MSD-Types registry, which RFC 8476 also points to for the equivalent OSPF extension.

sections.title: Why the Depth Has to Be Known
sections.content:
When Segment Routing paths are computed by a centralised controller, it is critical that the controller learns the Maximum SID Depth that can be imposed at each node or link on a given path. This ensures that the SID stack depth of a computed path does not exceed the number of SIDs the node is capable of imposing.

PCEP defines how to signal MSD in the Path Computation Element Communication Protocol. But if PCEP is not supported or configured on the head-end of an SR tunnel or a Binding-SID anchor node, and the controller does not take part in IGP routing, it has no way of learning the MSD of nodes and links. BGP-LS, the distribution of link-state and traffic engineering information using BGP, defines a way to expose topology and associated attributes and capabilities of the nodes to a centralised controller, and MSD signalling by BGP-LS has been defined separately. Typically, BGP-LS is configured on a small number of nodes that do not necessarily act as head-ends. For BGP-LS to signal MSD for all the nodes and links in the network where MSD matters, MSD capabilities should be advertised by every IS-IS router in the network.

Other kinds of MSD are known to be useful, such as Entropy Readable Label Depth, which a head-end uses to insert an entropy label at a depth where it can be read by transit nodes. This document defines an extension to IS-IS used to advertise one or more types of MSD at node and link granularity. It also creates an IANA registry for assigning MSD type identifiers and defines the Base MPLS Imposition type. It is expected that new types will later signal additional capabilities, such as entropy labels, SIDs imposed through recirculation, or SIDs for another data plane such as IPv6.

MSD advertisements may be useful even if Segment Routing itself is not enabled: in a non-SR MPLS network, MSD defines the maximum label depth.
sections.plainLanguage: A controller that builds a path out of numbered instructions needs to know how many instructions each router can hold. Without that number it can produce a path that no router can carry. IS-IS already tells routers about the topology, so it is the natural place to publish the depth as well.

sections.title: Terms Used Here
sections.content:
The RFC defines three terms of its own.

  • BMI, Base MPLS Imposition, is the number of MPLS labels that can be imposed, inclusive of all service, transport and special labels.
  • MSD, Maximum SID Depth, is the number of SIDs supported by a node or by a link on a node.
  • SID is the Segment Identifier defined in RFC 8402.

Label imposition is the act of modifying or adding labels to the outgoing label stack associated with a packet. It includes replacing the label at the top of the label stack with a new label, and pushing one or more new labels onto the label stack. The number of labels imposed is then the sum of the number of labels replaced and the number of labels pushed.
sections.plainLanguage: Two ideas matter. Maximum SID Depth is how many identifiers a router can carry. Label imposition is what a router does when it forwards a packet: it swaps the top label for another, pushes more labels on, or both. The depth limit counts both actions together.

sections.title: The Node MSD Sub-TLV
sections.content:
The Node MSD sub-TLV is defined within the body of the IS-IS Router CAPABILITY TLV to carry the provisioned SID depth of the router that originated that TLV. Node MSD is the smallest MSD supported by the node on the set of interfaces configured for use by the advertising IGP instance. The values may be learned through a hardware interface or provisioned.

The sub-TLV has a type of 23. Its length is variable, a multiple of 2 octets, representing the total length of the value field. The value field consists of one or more pairs, each a 1-octet MSD-Type followed by a 1-octet MSD-Value. The MSD-Type is a value defined in the IGP MSD-Types registry, which this document creates. The MSD-Value is a number in the range 0 to 255; for all MSD types, 0 represents the lack of ability to support a SID stack of any depth, and any other value represents that of the node. That value must represent the lowest value supported by any link configured for use by the advertising IS-IS instance.

The sub-TLV is optional, and the scope of the advertisement is specific to the deployment. If several Node MSD advertisements for the same MSD type originate from the same router, the procedures of RFC 7981 apply. Those procedures may result in different MSD values being used, for example by different controllers, but this does not create any interoperability issue.
sections.plainLanguage: The router publishes one number for itself, the depth it can manage across all of its interfaces. It sits inside the capability TLV that IS-IS routers already advertise. The value is a byte, so the range is 0 to 255, and zero means the router cannot carry a stack at all.

sections.title: The Link MSD Sub-TLV
sections.content:
The Link MSD sub-TLV is defined for TLVs 22, 23, 25, 141, 222 and 223 to carry the MSD of the interface associated with the link. The values may be signalled by the forwarding plane or may be provisioned.

The sub-TLV has a type of 15, with a variable length that is a multiple of 2 octets. The value field again consists of one or more pairs of a 1-octet MSD-Type and a 1-octet MSD-Value, with the type taken from the IGP MSD-Types registry. The MSD-Value is a number in the range 0 to 255; for all MSD types, 0 represents the lack of ability to support a SID stack of any depth, and any other value represents the depth of the particular link when used as an outgoing interface.

The sub-TLV is optional. If multiple Link MSD advertisements for the same MSD type and the same link are received, the procedure to select which copy to use is undefined.

If the advertising router performs label imposition in the context of the ingress interface, it is not possible to meaningfully advertise per-link values, and in that case only the Node MSD should be advertised.
sections.plainLanguage: A link can have a different limit from the router as a whole, so the link advertisement carries its own value. The number means the same thing everywhere: how deep a stack that interface can push. One case has no per-link meaning, and the RFC says to publish only the router-wide number there.

sections.title: Which Value to Use
sections.content:
When a Link MSD is present for a given MSD type, its value must take precedence over the Node MSD. When a Link MSD type is not signalled but the Node MSD type is, the Node MSD value must be used as the MSD value for that link.

In order to increase flooding efficiency, it is recommended that routers with homogeneous Link MSD values advertise just the Node MSD value, since a single advertisement then covers every link.

The meaning of the absence of both Node and Link MSD advertisements for a given MSD type is specific to that type. Generally, it can only be inferred that the advertising node does not support advertisement of that type. In some cases, however, the lack of advertisement might imply that the functionality associated with the type is not supported, and the correct interpretation must be specified when an MSD type is defined.
sections.plainLanguage: Two rules settle any question. A link value wins over the router value, and if there is no link value, the router value applies. A router whose links all behave the same is asked to advertise only the one number, to save flooding effort.

sections.title: The Base MPLS Imposition Depth
sections.content:
Base MPLS Imposition MSD, abbreviated BMI-MSD, signals the total number of MPLS labels that can be imposed, including all service, transport and special labels.

The absence of BMI-MSD advertisements indicates only that the advertising node does not support advertisement of this capability.
sections.plainLanguage: The first kind of depth to be defined counts every label a node can push, including the special ones used for services and transport. A node that says nothing about it is only saying that it does not publish the figure, not that it cannot push labels.

sections.title: Registry Allocations
sections.content:
IANA allocated a sub-TLV type from the Sub-TLVs for TLV 242, the IS-IS Router CAPABILITY TLV, registry defined by RFC 7981. The value 23 is allocated for the Node MSD sub-TLV.

IANA allocated a sub-TLV type from the Sub-TLVs for TLVs 22, 23, 25, 141, 222 and 223 registry, which covers the Extended IS reachability, IS Neighbor Attribute, L2 Bundle Member Attributes, inter-AS reachability information, MT-ISN and MT IS Neighbor Attribute TLVs. The value 15 is allocated for the Link MSD sub-TLV, and that sub-TLV may be present in all six of those TLVs.

IANA also created an IANA-managed registry titled IGP MSD-Types under the Interior Gateway Protocol Parameters registry, to identify the MSD types used in the Node and Link advertisements. The registration procedure is Expert Review as defined in RFC 8126, and types are an unsigned 8-bit number. The values defined by this document are 0 for Reserved, 1 for Base MPLS Imposition MSD, 2 to 250 unassigned, 251 to 254 for experimental use, and 255 for Reserved. General guidance for the designated experts is defined in RFC 7370.
sections.plainLanguage: Three things are registered. Sub-TLV 23 carries the router-wide depth inside the capability TLV, sub-TLV 15 carries the per-link depth inside the six link TLVs, and a new registry lists the kinds of depth: 1 is the plain MPLS depth, 251 to 254 are set aside for experiments, and the rest are unassigned.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations specified by RFC 7981 apply to this document.

Advertising an incorrect MSD value may have negative consequences. If the value is smaller than what is supported, path computation may fail to compute a viable path. If it is larger than what is supported, an attempt may occur to instantiate a path that the head-end, the node performing the SID imposition, cannot support. The presence of this information may also inform an attacker of how to induce either of those conditions.
sections.plainLanguage: The depth a router advertises is information an attacker could use, so a wrong value has real consequences: too small and the controller cannot build a path at all, too large and it builds one the router cannot carry.

How a receiver picks the value that applies to a link

items.title: Link value first
items.text: When a Link MSD is present for a type, its value takes precedence over the Node MSD.

items.title: Node value as fallback
items.text: When a link does not signal that type, the Node MSD value applies to that link.

items.title: One number is enough
items.text: Routers whose links all have the same value are asked to advertise only the Node MSD, which floods less.

items.title: Ingress imposition
items.text: A router that imposes labels on the incoming interface cannot give per-link values, so only the Node MSD should be advertised.
